leo.central_question: Why does lemon juice clean rust from iron, but baking soda make a burn stop stinging — and what do they have in common?
leo.essential_idea: Acids donate H⁺ ions and bases accept them — and when an acid meets a base, they cancel each other out to form a salt and water.

curiosity_hook.phenomenon: Red cabbage juice is purple. Add lemon juice: turns pink. Add baking soda water: turns green. Add both together until fizzing stops: turns purple again.
curiosity_hook.why_surprising: The same purple liquid transforms to pink, then to green, then back to original purple — purely from adding clear, colorless liquids. No dye was added. The color change came from chemistry, not pigment.
curiosity_hook.opening_image: A clear glass of deep purple liquid. A few drops of clear liquid added: liquid slowly shifts to bright pink. A few drops of another clear liquid: slowly shifts to vivid green. Pause. Then mixed together: slowly returns to purple.

common_misconceptions.statement: All acids burn and are dangerous; all bases are safe
common_misconceptions.why_believable: Students know acid burns from warning labels. Baking soda is used in kitchens — feels safe. The mental categories are 'dangerous acid' vs 'safe base'.

common_misconceptions.statement: Neutral means no acid and no base present
common_misconceptions.why_believable: Neutral sounds like 'empty' or 'nothing.' pH 7 sounds like the chemical equivalent of zero.

observation_sequence: Zinc metal added to hydrochloric acid: immediate fizzing, bubbles form, zinc dissolves. Gas collected and tested: burns with a pop — hydrogen.
Copper metal added to same acid: no reaction. No bubbles. Copper unchanged.
Sodium hydroxide solution added to hydrochloric acid drop by drop: no visible change. Temperature of mixture increases measurably.
Universal indicator added: at start deep red (acid). As base added: orange, yellow, green, blue. At exact neutralization point: green.

prediction_opportunities.moment: After seeing zinc react with acid but copper not react...
prediction_opportunities.question: What determines whether a metal reacts with acid?
options: The color of the metal — shiny metals react, dull metals don't
The reactivity of the metal — more reactive metals displace hydrogen from acid
The amount of acid — not enough acid for copper to react
prediction_opportunities.why_wrong_options_feel_right: Option A uses visual cues students rely on. Option C feels right because students have intuition that quantities matter.

concept_reveal.the_moment: The temperature rise during acid-base mixing reveals energy: neutralization is not just a color change — it releases heat. H⁺ and OH⁻ ions are so eager to form water that they release energy doing so. The pH indicator shows the battle; the thermometer shows the outcome.
concept_reveal.what_becomes_visible: Neutralization is a chemical battle between H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. When exactly equal numbers meet, they annihilate each other into water. The salt is just the leftover ions from both sides — neutral bystanders from the battle.

candidate_memory_models.name: The Tug of War
candidate_memory_models.description: H⁺ ions (acid team) and OH⁻ ions (base team) pull against each other. When the teams are equal, neither wins — the rope goes slack (neutralization). The spectators (Na⁺ and Cl⁻) who were cheering from the sidelines are left standing: they are the salt.
candidate_memory_models.why_memorable: Tug of war is a physical game Tamil students play. The 'spectator' ions become the salt — memorable role assignment.
candidate_memory_models.accuracy_note: Spectator ion model accurately describes neutralization for strong acid-strong base reactions.

real_world_connections.example: Applying toothpaste to a bee sting in Tamil Nadu — the alkaline paste neutralizes formic acid from sting
real_world_connections.connection_to_concept: Bee sting injects formic acid. Toothpaste (slightly alkaline) partially neutralizes it, reducing pain. Neutralization in a first-aid context.

real_world_connections.example: Adding tamarind (acidic) to dal — tastes sour because of tartaric acid
real_world_connections.connection_to_concept: Tamarind contains tartaric acid. The sour taste is a direct H⁺ ion sensation on taste receptors.

real_world_connections.example: Farmers in Tamil Nadu adding lime (calcium hydroxide) to acidic red soil before planting
real_world_connections.connection_to_concept: Acidic soil (pH < 6) is hostile to most crops. Lime (base) neutralizes soil acidity — agricultural neutralization at scale.

reflection_questions: Your stomach produces hydrochloric acid for digestion. Antacids are bases. Using neutralization, explain exactly how an antacid relieves indigestion.
Why do some fish die in lakes near coal plants? What is 'acid rain' and how does it use chemistry from this lesson?
A battery contains acid. A battery is also called a 'dry cell' or 'alkaline cell.' What do those names tell you about the chemistry inside?

memory_anchor.image_description: A glass of red cabbage juice: deep purple. Drop by drop of lemon juice added: slowly turns shocking pink. Then drop by drop of baking soda solution: slowly turns vivid green. Then both mixed together until fizzing stops: slowly returns to original purple.
memory_anchor.anchor_sentence: Red cabbage juice turns pink in acid, green in base, and purple again when they cancel out — because acids have H⁺ and bases have OH⁻, and together they make water.
memory_anchor.cognitive_hook: Color transformation is visually dramatic and memorable. The return to original purple creates a satisfying narrative arc. The cabbage juice is available in any kitchen — students can reproduce the experiment.

assessment_insight.understanding_vs_memorization: Memorization: pH scale, definitions of acid/base, salt examples. Understanding: Student predicts pH change from mixing, explains why neutralization releases heat, connects acid-base chemistry to biological contexts (stomach, blood pH).
assessment_insight.tn_board_pattern: 1-mark: Define acids and bases. Give pH of neutral solution. 3-mark: Explain neutralization with equation. Give examples of salts formed. 5-mark: Describe properties of acids and bases with examples. Explain pH scale with diagram.
assessment_insight.marks_tip: For neutralization equations: always write the full ionic equation as well as the molecular equation. TN Board frequently asks for both. Show H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O as the core neutralization alongside the full molecular equation.
